Fractal Optimization Through a Procedural Lens

Non-Euclidean geometry should be the base of mathematical understanding, and the same logic applies to non-integer dimensionality.

iori1

1Jorik Jonathan Chase, 3DIE — Design, Art & Technologies Label. Paper 0 of a series. October 2026.

Thank you to all those who stand by me.

The paper in one paragraph

Look closely at a coastline, a tree or a cloud and the detail does not run out. This paper is about that roughness: how to measure it, the simplest machine that makes it, and what it means for the machines that now make pictures. The machine is Brownian motion, a walk of random steps. Run forwards, it roughens. Run backwards, it is what an image generator does when it turns noise into a picture. The paper's own result is a short proof of two things everyone who watches a generator notices: it draws the large shapes first and the details last, and one recipe works at every zoom. Both follow from one fact about the world, that it is rough in the same proportion at every scale.

Every figure runs in the page. The mathematics sits folded under the text in boxes marked The mathematics; nothing in the text depends on opening them. Words with a dotted line are in the glossary.

1. Fractals

A fractal is a shape whose detail does not run out when you zoom in. Its dimension says how fast the detail grows.

1.1 How Long Is a Coastline?

Richardson measured coastlines with a pair of dividers and found that the answer depends on the dividers. Set them to 100 km and walk the coast of Britain: so many steps. Set them to 10 km and the walk goes into bays the long steps cut across, and the coast is longer. It keeps getting longer as the ruler shrinks, with no sign of stopping [1]. Mandelbrot read Richardson's table in 1967 and saw that the way the length grows is the thing to measure [2].

The Koch curve does it exactly [3]. Replace a segment by four segments a third as long, and repeat on every segment. Each round multiplies the length by 4/3, forever. Below, walk it with a ruler of your own. Halve the ruler and the measured length grows by the same factor every time; on the log plot the points fall on a line, and the slope of that line is the dimension minus one. Between the powers of three the measure wobbles, which real coastlines also do; the fit uses the powers.

The mathematics

A shape made of N copies of itself, each scaled by 1/r, has similarity dimension D = log N / log r. For a line, 2 copies at ½: D = 1. For a square, 4 at ½: 2. For the Koch curve, 4 at ⅓: log 4 / log 3 = 1.262.

Measured with a ruler of length ε, the curve takes n(ε) ∝ ε−D steps, so its length is

L(ε) = ε · n(ε) ∝ ε1 − D.

A smooth curve has D = 1 and a length that stops changing. Richardson found exponents 1 − D of about −0.25 for the west coast of Britain and close to 0 for South Africa's.

1.2 The Sierpinski Carpet

Cut a square into nine, remove the middle one, repeat on the eight that remain. Each round keeps 8 copies at a third of the size, so D = log 8 / log 3 = 1.893: more than a line, less than a plane. The Mandelbrot set is the same idea with a different rule. Mirrorbrot [4] folds it, the 16K edition [5] pushes the zoom, and the Nebulabrot [6] draws the escape paths instead of the boundary.

1.3 The Menger Sponge

The same cut in three dimensions keeps 20 cubes of 27, D = log 20 / log 3 = 2.727. Drag to rotate. It is also the first, smallest example of what self-similarity buys. The sponge is drawn as copies of one cube, so the work grows with the 20 cubes kept, not the 27 cells of a grid; at level 3 that is 8,000 cubes against 19,683 cells, and the gap widens by 27/20 every level. Chapter 6 is the large version of this. The N-Dimensional Viewer [7] slices fractals in more dimensions, and the tesseract [8] shows what one slice of a 4D object loses.

2. Brownian Motion: The Casebook

Mandelbrot's Fractal Geometry of Nature is a casebook: a chapter per phenomenon. Most of the phenomena are one machine, the random walk, with one dial turned.

This chapter is that casebook, live [9]. Each section turns one dial and names the dimension it produces.

2.1 The Random Walk

Each step moves up to 5 pixels in a random direction. Stretch time by a factor c and the path stretches by √c, so no zoom looks different from any other: the walk is self-similar by construction. Its trail has dimension 2 in the plane. Measure it: a short walk reads lower and climbs toward 2 as it fills the square. Diffusion Fluid [10] is the same walk run as a field.

2.2 Fractional Brownian Motion

Mandelbrot and Van Ness put a dial on the walk, the Hurst exponent H [11]. Above ½ the steps remember each other and the trace is smooth and persistent; below ½ they contradict each other and it is rough; at ½ it is Brownian. The graph has dimension 2 − H. Hurst found the dial in eight centuries of Nile flood records, at H ≈ 0.7 [12]. The seed below is the same at every H, so the slider changes only the roughness.

2.3 Brownian Landscapes and Coastlines

The same construction on a grid gives Mandelbrot's Brownian landscapes, relief of dimension 3 − H [13]. Flood it to the mean height and the shore is a coastline of dimension 2 − H: section 1.1 again, grown instead of drawn. Every terrain in every game is this machine.

2.4 Lévy Flights

Keep the walk and drop the typical step. Draw the step lengths from a power law and the walk becomes a Lévy flight: clusters of clusters of visits, which Mandelbrot called Lévy dust and used for the distribution of galaxies. With exponent α below 2 the dust has dimension α. Above 2 a typical step returns and the walk is Brownian again.

2.5 Diffusion-Limited Aggregation

Release a Brownian walker far from a seed, let it stick when it touches the cluster, repeat. Witten and Sander: the aggregate has dimension 1.71 [14]. The button gives three numbers. Mass against radius reads 1.63 to 1.70 on this small lattice. Box counting reads about 1.5, because at two cells a branch is a line. Box counting capped at a quarter of the cluster radius is the lesson Petri [15] paid for: on its grid, boxes near the cluster's own size dragged the slope toward 2.

2.6 Trees and Forests: Synthetic Silviculture

A tree is a branching fractal, but nobody draws it. It grows. Buds compete for light, the well-lit branches get more of the plant's vigour, the shaded ones are shed, and the crown ends up filling the light it can reach. Pałubicki and colleagues grew single trees from those rules [16], with the vigour split between leader and side branch taken from Borchert and Honda's measurements of a tropical tree [17]. Makowski, Pałubicki and colleagues then grew whole forests and called it synthetic silviculture [18]: modules of branches grow by the light they receive, every plant shades its neighbours, grown trees seed young ones around them, and plants die of age or of shade.

Nothing in the rules says forest. Pioneers that need full light come first; shade-tolerant trees germinate under them and take over; the stand thins as it grows. Foresters measured that thinning long before computers: in a crowded stand, mean plant mass rises as density to the power −3/2 [19]. Makowski's full model reproduces that law. The reduced one here does not, cleanly: dense even-aged plantations thin at slopes between −2.3 and −3.1, steeper than the foresters' −3/2, and the mixed forest loops in the second chart as pioneer cohorts boom and bust every fifty years or so. It drops the paper's branch prototypes and climate, and adds three rules of its own; the gap is the price of that. A tree is a shape that is also a search, which is where chapter 4 starts.

2.7 The Spectrum of a Rough World

A rough world leaves a signature you can measure on any photograph. Break a picture into layers from the broadest shapes to the finest grain and ask how loud each layer is. That is its power spectrum. For a rough world the answer is a straight line on log scales: every octave finer is quieter by the same factor. Field found power falling as 1/fβ with β close to 2 [20]; Ruderman and Bialek measured 1.81 in woodland [21]; Torralba and Oliva fitted twelve thousand scenes at 1.8 to 2.4 depending on scene and direction [22].

The photograph below is the iris behind eye 26 of the Iris Engine (Lizapopova143, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 4.0). Its texture reads about 2.9 and the whole iris 2.7, steeper than the scene average because one object at one distance is smoother than a scene. The carpet reads 2.35. The landscape from 2.3 should read 2H + 2 and midpoint displacement comes in a little under. White noise reads 0. Every one of them is a straight line, and that is the point. Now move the noise slider: noise is equally loud at every layer, the flat blue line, and every layer under it is gone. Keep this picture; chapter 5 is built on it.

3. Measuring Roughness

Two tools carry every number in this paper: one finds the edges, the other counts boxes.

3.1 Difference of Gaussians

Blur the image twice with different widths and subtract. What survives is edges, the Marr–Hildreth operator [23]. Here the two blurs are box blurs, a cheap stand-in for the Gaussians. Upload your own image, or use the sample: the carpet from 1.2 at level 4.

3.2 Box Counting

Cover the edges with boxes of side 2, 4, 8, 16, 32 and 64 pixels, count the boxes that touch an edge, and fit log count against log 1/size. The slope is D. The carpet's answer is known, 1.893; the counter reads 1.81. The gap is the method. The smallest boxes see pixel-wide edges, dimension 1; the largest see the whole image, dimension 2; only the middle of the range sees the carpet. A dimension is never read off one number. It is read off a range of scales, and the range has to be stated.

4. Walks That Fit

The world is rough, and a model has to fit it. Every fitter I know is a walk on a rough landscape.

4.1 The Ising Model and Annealing

Spins on a 100 × 100 grid, each up or down, each wanting to match its four neighbours. The Metropolis rule [24]: a flip that lowers the energy is always taken, one that raises it by ΔE is taken with probability exp(−ΔE/T). Onsager solved this grid exactly [25]: the critical temperature is 2 / ln(1 + √2) = 2.269. The slider starts at 2.3. Below it the domains freeze, above it there is only noise, and at it there are domains of every size: the fractal case. Beggs and Plenz measured the same power law in the avalanches of living cortex [26]. Press Anneal: start hot, cool slowly [27], and the domains grow instead of freezing where they stand.

4.2 A Walker on a Rough Landscape

Take the trace from 2.2 as a landscape and drop a Metropolis walker on it: down is free, up costs exp(−ΔE/T). Cold, it sits in the first dip it finds. Hot, it wanders and settles nowhere. Anneal, and it finds the deep one more often than not. This is all of optimisation on a fractal. The roughness is at every scale, so there is no scale at which a greedy step is safe.

4.3 The Fitters

The Iris Engine [28] fits a procedural iris to a photograph: a search over the shape genes, a material inversion per cell, two thousand Gaussian splats on the relief by gradient descent, then the layer model. On the four isolated eyes the match score reads 90.35, 88.12, 91.40 and 88.32, and the shipped files reproduce those renders within one level on every load. That walk has no noise in it. The splat scenes [29] will be trained with MCMC splatting [30], which is stochastic gradient Langevin dynamics [31]: gradient plus Brownian noise, the walker from 4.2 on millions of parameters. Petri's think tank runs CMA-ES [32], Gaussian mutations on a genome. Evolution is the original [33].

5. Why Image Generators Draw the Big Shapes First

An image generator starts from pure noise and removes it a little at a time. Watch one work and the large shapes come first, the details last. This chapter proves why, in four steps, and each step is a figure.

The argument without mathematics

  1. Noise is equally loud at every scale. On the spectrum plot of 2.7 it is a flat line.
  2. The world is not. Every scale finer is quieter by the same factor. On the plot, a falling straight line.
  3. Noise drowns the quiet scales first. Pour noise on a photograph and the finest grain goes under at the first drop; the continents only at the very end. The best possible guess of the picture under the noise keeps the scales still louder than the noise and has to give up the rest.
  4. A generator runs that backwards. It lowers the noise step by step, so it can only settle the scales in the opposite order: continents first, grain last.

And because every scale is quieter than the last by the same factor, halving the noise always uncovers the same number of new scales, whether you are at the continents or at the grain. That is why one schedule, one recipe for how fast to lower the noise, serves every zoom.

5.1 Is the Noise in Stable Diffusion Brownian?

For the models most people have used, yes. Stable Diffusion 1.x, 2.x and XL add noise in a thousand small Gaussian steps to a compressed 64 × 64 × 4 picture [34][35]. Those steps are the discrete form of an Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process, Brownian motion with a gentle pull toward zero [36][37]. Stable Diffusion 3 and FLUX do not walk. They slide along a straight line from the picture to one draw of noise [38]. What every family shares is the state at each noise level: the picture plus Gaussian noise of a known width σ. The proof below is written in σ, so it covers all of them.

5.2 The Four Steps, Live

The figure is a world whose spectrum you choose, the exponent β. On the left the world, in the middle what the generator sees at noise level σ, on the right the best possible guess of the world from what it sees. The chart is steps 1 to 3 at once: the falling line is the world, the flat line is the noise, and the shaded band is what the best guess can still recover. Press Generate and σ falls the way a generator lowers it. At β = 2 the picture arrives continents first. Set β to 0, a world as loud at every scale as the noise itself, and press Generate again: there is no order any more, every scale arrives at once.

5.3 The Theorem

Let a world x be a stationary Gaussian field whose power spectrum falls as a power law, S(f) = A f−β with β > 0, and let it be seen as y = x + σz under white Gaussian noise of width σ.

  1. The best guess of x from y keeps every frequency f in proportion S/(S + σ²). This is Tweedie's formula, and here it is the Wiener filter.
  2. A frequency is half kept and half lost exactly at the cutoff f*(σ) = (A/σ²)1/β. Below the cutoff the world is mostly known; above it, mostly noise.
  3. As σ falls the cutoff rises, so any process that lowers the noise settles the frequencies in increasing order: coarse to fine.
  4. Lowering σ by any factor is the same filter, dilated. Each halving of σ uncovers 2/β octaves, the same number at every scale. For β = 2, one halving of the noise is one new octave of detail, everywhere.
The mathematics: proof

Independence. A stationary field is diagonal in the Fourier basis: each frequency is an independent Gaussian coordinate with variance S(f). White noise adds an independent coordinate of variance σ² to each. So the whole problem splits into one scalar problem per frequency, yf = xf + σzf.

(1) For one Gaussian coordinate the posterior mean is

E[xf | yf] = S(f) / (S(f) + σ²) · yf.

Tweedie's formula says the same thing without the Gaussian assumption on the world: the best guess is E[x|y] = y + σ² ∇ log p(y) [39]. Here p(y) is Gaussian with spectrum S + σ², so ∇ log p multiplies frequency f by −1/(S + σ²), and y − σ²y/(S + σ²) = S y/(S + σ²). The gradient term is the score, the thing a diffusion network is trained to output; Wiener wrote the filter in 1949 [40].

(2) The gain is ½ where S(f) = σ², that is A f−β = σ², so f* = (A/σ²)1/β. What is left unknown about frequency f after seeing y is the posterior variance Sσ²/(S + σ²): close to σ² (settled up to the noise) below the cutoff, close to S (nothing learned) above it.

(3) f* falls as σ grows, so it rises as σ falls. The reverse process of a diffusion model is the time reversal of the forward one, and its drift is the score [41]. At every point of the reverse path the state is a picture at some level σ, and by (2) only the frequencies below f*(σ) are determined there. So they are determined in increasing order.

(4) Write Hσ(f) = S/(S + σ²). Then

Hλσ(f) = Hσ(λ2/βf), so f*(λσ) = λ−2/β f*(σ).

With λ = ½ the cutoff moves up by 22/β, which is 2/β octaves, independent of σ. A schedule uniform in log σ therefore uncovers octaves at a constant rate. ∎

5.4 From the Theorem to Real Pictures

Photographs are not Gaussian fields: they have edges and objects. Three things carry the theorem over. The spectrum of photographs is a power law with β near 2, measured, not proved (section 2.7). Trained denoisers act like adaptive versions of this filter, keeping coefficients louder than the noise in a basis fitted to the image [42]. And the generated order is observed: Rissanen and colleagues reported that diffusion models generate coarse to fine [43], and Dieleman named it spectral autoregression [44].

Where the theorem stands among them. Rissanen gave the additive noise floor, Dieleman the phrase, Falck and colleagues the signal-to-noise picture per frequency [45], and Hunt, Kamb and Ganguli wrote the power-law Wiener filter and its rescaling [46]. None of them states the order of generation as a theorem. The contribution here is that statement with the schedule corollary, and figures that let anyone check it.

Two limits keep it honest. Falck's group built a forward process that noises every frequency equally, and it trains as well as the usual one. So the coarse-to-fine order is a consequence of Gaussian noise meeting a power-law world, not a condition for diffusion to work at all. And production schedules do shift with resolution: SD3 shifts by a factor of 3 at 1024², FLUX by the number of tokens. That fits the theorem rather than breaking it. Changing the pixel count moves every frequency in pixel units, and the theorem's statement is in units of the picture.

5.5 The Carpet From Noise

The last figure leaves the Gaussian world. The data are 1,200 points on the carpet, shown faintly; 1,200 points start as noise. Each step runs the reverse-time equation one level down the schedule, with the exact score of the noised data, computed from the points instead of learned by a network. Watch the order in which the carpet returns: the big hole first, then the eight, then the sixty-four. That order is the theorem, on a world that is a fractal instead of a Gaussian field.

The mathematics: the sampler

The forward process adds Gaussian noise of growing width σ. For data points x1 … xM, the noised density is a sum of Gaussians and its score is exact:

∇ log pσ(x) = Σi wi (xi − x) / σ², w = softmax(−|x − xi|² / 2σ²).

One reverse step from σk to σk+1 is x ← x + (σk² − σk+1²) ∇ log p + √(σk² − σk+1²) z, the Euler–Maruyama step of Anderson's reverse equation [37]. A network learns the score; nothing else changes.

6. What the Fractal Toolset Buys: Speed

Self-similarity is also a shortcut. Where a problem has the same structure at every scale, the work can be done once per scale instead of once per pair.

Below are a few thousand bodies scattered as Lévy dust, clusters of clusters. Each pulls on every other, so the direct sum is one interaction per pair: N². Barnes and Hut group the far bodies into boxes of a quadtree and let one box stand for all of its contents when it looks small from where you stand [47]. The opening angle θ says how small is small. The count falls to about N log N. At 4,000 bodies and θ = 0.5 the tree does 41 times less work for an error of 0.9 %; at 32,000 bodies, 235 times less for 2 %. The bigger the problem, the bigger the gain. Push θ past 1 and the error climbs to 5 and then 10 %: the shortcut only holds while a far box really does look small.

The same trade runs through all fast numerical methods. Each buys its speed with one regularity across scales, and each fails where that regularity fails.

MethodWorkThe regularity it needs
Fast Fourier transform [48]N² → N log Nthe transform factors into log N sparse layers
Multigrid [49]→ Nafter smoothing, the error is smooth and a coarser grid can fix it; Petri's pressure solver is one
Fast multipole [50]N² → Na far cluster's pull compresses to a few terms
Wavelets [51]→ Nnested scales, each half the last
Hierarchical matrices [52]n³ → n k² log² noff-diagonal blocks are nearly low-rank
Monarch and butterfly layers [53]n² → n√na weight matrix close to a product of block-diagonal ones; GPT-2 trained 2× faster
Instancing (1.3)27ⁿ → 20ⁿexact self-similarity

None of it makes an arbitrary shape faster. Recursion is cheap only where the structure is really there. For neural networks the open question is the landscape. Sohl-Dickstein found that the boundary between training that converges and training that diverges is fractal in the plane of learning rates, with box dimensions from 1.17 to 1.98 [54]. Stochastic gradient descent behaves, under four stated assumptions, like the walker of 4.2 at a temperature set by learning rate over batch size [55]. Whether that landscape has a regularity a fast method can use is the subject of paper 2.

7. Consequences

Every fit is the same act: a slow walk of a model toward a rough world.

The context an organism adapts to is not a problem with a solution. It is a fitness landscape [33], and the landscape is rugged at every scale: a niche as intricate at the scale of a biome as at the edge of one leaf. Evolution is not a climb. It is a population diffusing across that surface, the walk from 2.1 with selection as its drift. The butterfly's wing and the perceptron's learned weights [56] are two snapshots of the same walk: the slow, painful, and finally beautiful convergence of a model to a world.

Every engine on this site is that act. An iris ID, a Dish ID and a flame preset are compact descriptions, and each engine regenerates a world from one. What none of them has yet is a sense of which descriptions are likely, learned from the fitted cases, and a noisy walk to sample them: diffusion over the description instead of the pixels, with the engine in the loop. The honest gap is size. The fitted set is four eyes. The step this paper implies is the database of fitted eyes the Iris Engine was planned around, and a score learned over it. Then an eye from zero is the carpet from noise.

8. The Series

Brownian motion makes a rough world. A cellular automaton computes one. This paper opens a series, and its last section is a pointer to each of the others.

8.1 Towards the Computational Basis

The next paper, Cellular Automata as the Computational Basis [57], takes local rules as the subject. Conway's rule [58]: a live cell survives with two or three live neighbours and a dead one is born with three. Langton's ant [59]: on white turn right, on black turn left, flip the cell, step; ten thousand steps of mess, then a highway.

Flame Strains [61] burns any 2D automaton as a strain inside one volumetric flame. Petri runs ten growth kernels and 93 organisms as data rows, every dish replayable bit for bit. Its first measured result opens the next paper: Tero and colleagues let Physarum connect 36 food sources laid out as the cities around Tokyo [62], and Petri's adaptive Physarum on Tero's own geometry, 21 replicates, bands fixed before the run, lands inside the published spread.

Petri (n = 21)Tero 2010
total length / minimum tree1.80 ± 0.261.75 ± 0.30
minimum distance / minimum tree0.835 ± 0.0400.85 ± 0.04
fault tolerance0.854 ± 0.0500.86 ± 0.04

Slime Mold [63], Ember Engine [64], Mycelium [65] and Frost [66] are the single-rule engines before Petri.

Glossary

Dimension (fractal)
How fast the detail of a shape grows as you zoom in. A line is 1, a plane is 2; a coastline is in between. Measured as the slope of count against scale on log axes.
Self-similar
Looks the same at every zoom, exactly (the carpet) or statistically (a Brownian walk). Self-affine: the same after stretching the two axes by different amounts, like the trace in 2.2.
Brownian motion
A walk of independent random steps. The simplest machine that makes a rough world, and the noise of the older image generators.
Hurst exponent H
The roughness dial of a walk. ½ is Brownian; above ½ the steps remember each other and the trace is smoother; below ½ it is rougher.
Power spectrum
How loud each scale of a picture or a signal is, from the broadest shapes to the finest grain. A rough world has a spectrum that is a straight falling line on log axes.
Octave
A doubling of frequency, or a halving of scale. From continents to countries is one octave if countries are half the size.
Noise level σ
The width of the Gaussian noise on a picture at one moment of a diffusion model. Generation lowers it from large to nearly zero along a schedule.
Score
The direction in which a noisy picture becomes more likely, ∇ log p. A diffusion network is trained to output it; by Tweedie's formula it is the best guess of the clean picture, minus the noisy one, over σ².
Annealing
Searching hot, then cooling slowly, so a walker can leave shallow dips early and settle into a deep one late.
